title: Fourier Transform
body:
A [[Fourier Series]] decomposes a **periodic** function into a discrete set of frequencies. The
Fourier transform does the same job for a function that never repeats, and the price is that the
discrete set becomes a continuum:

$$
\hat{f}(\xi) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,e^{-2\pi i x \xi}\,dx
\qquad
f(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \hat{f}(\xi)\,e^{2\pi i x \xi}\,d\xi
$$

The forward transform takes a signal in time (or space) and returns its **spectrum**: how much of
each frequency $\xi$ is present, as a complex number carrying amplitude in its magnitude and phase
in its argument. The inverse puts it back, and the only difference between the two formulas is the
sign in the exponent.

## Where it comes from

Take a [[Fourier Series]] on $[-L/2, L/2]$ and let $L \to \infty$. The allowed frequencies are
spaced $1/L$ apart, so as the period grows the spacing shrinks to zero, the sum becomes an integral,
and the coefficients $c_n$ become the continuous function $\hat{f}(\xi)$. **A non-periodic signal is
a periodic one whose period is infinite**, and that is the entire derivation in one sentence.

| | [[Fourier Series]] | Fourier transform | [[Discrete Fourier Transform]] |
|---|---|---|---|
| Input | periodic, continuous | non-periodic, continuous | finite sample vector |
| Output | discrete coefficients $c_n$ | continuous spectrum $\hat{f}(\xi)$ | finite vector of $N$ values |
| Machinery | integral over one period | integral over $\mathbb{R}$ | sum over $N$ samples |
| Computable? | by hand | by hand | **by machine**, via [[Fast Fourier Transform]] |

## Properties table

These are what the transform is *for*: each one turns an awkward operation in one domain into an
easy one in the other.

| Operation on $f$ | Effect on $\hat{f}$ | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Linearity: $af + bg$ | $a\hat{f} + b\hat{g}$ | superposition survives the transform |
| Time shift: $f(x - a)$ | $e^{-2\pi i a\xi}\hat{f}(\xi)$ | delay changes phase only, never magnitude |
| Modulation: $e^{2\pi i a x}f(x)$ | $\hat{f}(\xi - a)$ | multiplying by a carrier slides the spectrum. This is AM radio |
| Scaling: $f(ax)$ | $\frac{1}{\|a\|}\hat{f}(\xi/a)$ | **squeeze in time, stretch in frequency**. A short pulse is broadband |
| Derivative: $f'(x)$ | $2\pi i \xi\,\hat{f}(\xi)$ | differentiation becomes multiplication |
| Convolution: $f * g$ | $\hat{f}\cdot\hat{g}$ | see [[Convolution Theorem]] |

**The derivative property is the reason engineers use this on differential equations.** A linear
ODE with constant coefficients becomes a polynomial equation in $\xi$: solve algebraically, then
invert. Applied to a PDE it removes one variable entirely, which is the transform method sitting
beside separation of variables in [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]]. The Laplace transform is the same
manoeuvre with a different kernel and one-sided limits; the vault has no note for it.

**The scaling property is an uncertainty principle.** You cannot make a signal narrow in time and
narrow in frequency at once. A [[Dirac Delta Function]] is a single instant and its transform is
flat across all frequencies; a pure sine wave lasts forever and its transform is a single spike.
Everything real is between the two, and this trade-off is what [[Wavelet Transform]] in
[[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]] exists to manage.

## Related

- [[Complex Exponential]] for why $e^{-2\pi i x\xi}$ rather than sines and cosines.
- [[Parseval's Identity]] holds here too: $\int|f|^2 = \int|\hat{f}|^2$.
- [[Sampling Theorem]] is the bridge from this to anything a computer can hold.
